title: Chapter 145 — Managing Delivery Delays
intro: The manufacturer pushed the ship date. The truck broke down. Whatever the reason — the customer is waiting.

sections.title: Breaking the News
sections.content:
Call, do not email. And call before the customer calls you. The customer who discovers a delivery delay by waiting all day for a truck that never comes will never fully trust you again. The customer who gets a proactive call at 8 AM still has time to adjust their day.

'Hi [name], I am calling about your delivery scheduled for Thursday. Unfortunately, [reason — be specific, not vague]. I am sorry — I know you were counting on this. Here is what I can do.'

Be specific about the reason. 'The manufacturer delayed shipment' is better than 'there has been a delay.' Specificity shows you actually know what happened and are managing it, not just relaying bad news from someone else.

Always have the next step ready before you make the call. Do not call with bad news and no solution. Call with bad news AND an updated timeline.

sections.title: What to Offer
sections.content:
Updated timeline with a firm commitment — not 'sometime next week' but 'Thursday between 10 and 2.' If you cannot give a firm date yet, give a firm date for when you will have a firm date.

Loaner options if available and if the customer is without an essential appliance — no fridge for two weeks is a crisis, not an inconvenience. Some stores have loaner units for exactly this situation.

Partial credit or accommodation for the inconvenience — a delivery fee waiver, a gift card, an accessory thrown in. The gesture matters more than the dollar amount. It says 'we know this cost you time and frustration.'

Expedited delivery when available — bump them to the next available slot ahead of the queue. The customer who was delayed should be first in line, not last.

sections.title: Preventing the Cascade
sections.content:
A delivery delay becomes a lost sale or chargeback through a predictable cascade: delay happens → silence from the store → customer calls and gets voicemail → customer calls again and gets a vague answer → customer loses confidence → customer cancels and buys elsewhere → customer leaves a review about the experience.

Break the cascade at step one: communicate proactively. Break it at step two: give specific answers. Break it at step three: provide a concrete next step and a timeline.

The customers you lose to delivery delays are not lost because of the delay itself — they are lost because of the silence that followed the delay. A customer who is informed, updated, and given options will wait. A customer who feels ignored will leave.
